chapters.title: Chapter 2: Price Formation, Spreads and Liquidity

lessons.title: Tick Size, Price-Time Priority and Queue Position Mechanics

body.text: Tick size is not a rounding convention, it is a structural knob that sets the minimum possible spread and, by forcing every trader who wants roughly the same price into the exact same queue, determines how much your position in time actually matters.

children.text: Tick size is the smallest price increment an exchange allows an order to be priced at. NSE's standard equity tick size is ₹0.05, which means two orders that a trader might mentally think of as offering roughly the same price, one at ₹2,449.97 and one at ₹2,449.99, are both illegal quotes; both get rounded into the exchange's actual grid of allowed prices. This has a direct mechanical consequence covered in Chapter 1: the spread between the best bid and best ask can never be narrower than one tick, no matter how many participants would genuinely be willing to trade at a price in between.
The Tick Size Trade-off: Too Wide vs Too Narrow

Regulators and exchanges globally have run real experiments on this trade-off, including the US SEC's Tick Size Pilot from 2016 to 2018, which widened ticks for a set of small-cap stocks specifically to study the effect. A tick that is too large relative to a stock's natural price granularity forces a wider minimum spread than the stock would otherwise need, which raises trading costs for everyone. But it also makes price improvement expensive: undercutting the best bid or ask by a full tick is a real, visible concession, so participants compete mainly on being early rather than on shaving price, and queue position becomes genuinely valuable. A tick that is too small lets anyone leapfrog the front of a queue by improving price by a negligible amount, which discourages traders from resting large size at any one level, since it can be cheaply jumped, and tends to thin out displayed depth.

cells: Minimum spread wider than the stock's natural price granularity would need
Price improvement is expensive; participants compete mainly on arrival time, so queue position matters a great deal
Spread can compress toward the stock's true granularity
Tiny price improvements can cheaply leapfrog a queue, discouraging large resting size and thinning displayed depth

body.text: NSE applies a uniform ₹0.05 tick size across most equity cash market scrips, but exact tick sizes for specific segments such as low-priced stocks, ETFs, and individual F&O contracts are set by exchange circulars and can differ or change. Confirm the current tick size for a specific instrument against the live exchange contract specifications rather than assuming it here.

markDefs.definition: Where an order sits, in arrival order, among all other resting orders at the same price level. Earlier arrival means earlier fill when an opposing order matches at that price; queue position is invisible in standard Level 2 depth data, which shows only aggregate quantity per level.

children.text: Say the best bid for a stock is ₹1,842.30, and four separate limit buy orders are resting there, in this arrival order: Order A for 1,200 shares, Order B for 800 shares, your order C for 2,000 shares, and Order D for 1,500 shares, all at the identical price. Price-time priority means a matching sell order fills against A first, then B, then your order C, then D, strictly in arrival order, never by size, never by any factor except who got there first at that price. If a market sell order for 3,000 shares arrives, it fully fills A's 1,200 and B's 800, using up 2,000 of the 3,000 shares, and then fills exactly 1,000 of your 2,000-share order before running out of quantity. You end up with 1,000 shares filled and 1,000 shares still resting, now at the very front of the queue, while Order D behind you gets nothing at all from this particular sell order.

body.code:
class PriceLevelQueue:
    """A single price level's resting orders, in strict arrival order."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.orders = []  # list of [order_id, qty], append order = arrival order

    def add(self, order_id, qty):
        self.orders.append([order_id, qty])

    def match(self, incoming_qty):
        filled = {}
        i = 0
        while incoming_qty > 0 and i < len(self.orders):
            order_id, qty = self.orders[i]
            take = min(qty, incoming_qty)
            filled[order_id] = filled.get(order_id, 0) + take
            self.orders[i][1] -= take
            incoming_qty -= take
            i += 1
        self.orders = [o for o in self.orders if o[1] > 0]  # drop fully filled orders
        return filled

queue = PriceLevelQueue()
queue.add("A", 1200)
queue.add("B", 800)
queue.add("C", 2000)   # your order
queue.add("D", 1500)

print(queue.match(3000))
# {'A': 1200, 'B': 800, 'C': 1000}
body.caption: A minimal FIFO simulation of price-time priority at one price level. Order C, the example order from the text above, gets partially filled exactly as worked out by hand.

children.text: Why Placement Timing Matters Even Without HFT Infrastructure

You do not need colocation to benefit from this. The moment a stock's price moves to a new level, its queue at that price starts empty, and the first realistic window to be near the front of a fresh queue is right when it forms, not minutes later once it may already hold thousands of shares from other traders. A limit order placed the instant a new best price appears earns a meaningfully better queue position than the identical order placed even a few seconds later once other resting size has piled in ahead of it. This single mechanical fact is also the foundation for a real short-horizon alpha idea, queue position alpha, that Chapter 4 builds out properly once order flow and imbalance signals are in place.

body.text: Two orders at the identical price are not the same order. The one that arrived earlier has a strictly better claim on the next matching trade, and that claim is worth real money on a stock that trades frequently, even though nothing about price or quantity distinguishes the two orders on a standard Level 2 screen.

body.title: Working Out a Partial Fill
body.prompt: At the best ask of a stock, three sell orders rest in arrival order: 500 shares, then 1,500 shares (this one is yours), then 900 shares. A market buy order for 1,300 shares arrives. How many shares of your 1,500-share order get filled?
body.explanation: The incoming 1,300-share buy order fills the first order's 500 shares completely, using 500 of the 1,300. The remaining 800 shares then fill against your order next in the queue, leaving 700 of your 1,500 shares still resting and the 900-share order behind you completely untouched.

body.title: What Determines Fill Order at the Same Price
body.question: Two limit orders rest at the identical best bid price on NSE, one for 5,000 shares and one for 500 shares placed a fraction of a second later. A matching sell order for 500 shares arrives. Which order gets filled first?
options: The larger order, since exchanges prioritize bigger orders to reduce the number of trades
The smaller order, since it can be filled completely in one match
The order that arrived first, regardless of its size, since NSE uses strict price-time priority
Both orders are filled proportionally to their size
body.explanation: Price-time priority uses arrival time as the only tiebreaker among orders at the same price, order size plays no role at all. The order that arrived first is filled first, in full, before the exchange moves on to the next order in the queue, which is exactly the mechanic simulated in this lesson's code example.

points: Tick size sets the minimum possible spread by forcing every order into a discrete price grid; on NSE equities that grid is typically ₹0.05
Too wide a tick raises trading costs but makes queue position valuable; too narrow a tick lets cheap price improvement leapfrog queues and thins displayed depth
Price-time priority fills resting orders at a price level strictly by arrival time, never by size
A partial fill against a large resting order leaves the remainder at the front of the queue, ahead of everyone who arrived after it
Queue position is invisible in standard Level 2 depth data, which shows only aggregate quantity per price level, not individual order arrival order

Placing a limit order the instant a new best price forms captures a better queue position than the same order placed even seconds later, and this fact underlies the queue position alpha idea developed in Chapter 4
